text:
Citation:

Citizens v.
Canadian Jewish Congress

D
ate:  20000503

2000 BCSC 737

Docket:

98/2800

Registry:
Victoria

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:

citizens for foreign aid reform
inc.

plaintiff

AND:

canadian jewish congress AND

michael elterman

defendants

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT

OF THE

HONOURABLE mr. JUSTICE mckinnon

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

D.
Christie

Counsel for the Defendants:

P.
Gordon

Date and Place of Hearing/Trial:

March
21, 2000

Victoria,
BC

[
1
]

The plaintiff claims damages for defamation by
the Canadian Jewish Congress (the Congress) and the named defendant, Dr.
Michael Elterman.

[
2
]

The alleged defamation is contained within a
document entitled, “Issues of Concern to the Jewish Community of British
Columbia 1995-98”.   A paragraph in that document describes the plaintiff (and
others) as a “white supremacist hate group that directs violence and hate
propaganda towards Jews and others".  In a “Forward” to this document, Dr. Michael
Elterman describes himself as “Chair, Canadian Jewish Congress Pacific
Region”.  The “Forward” describes this group as a “regional branch" of the
defendant Congress and one which, “maintains close links with all provincial
political parties and all levels of government”.

[
3
]

In the motions before me, the plaintiff seeks to
compel Dr. Elterman to answer a series of questions he refused to answer on his
examination for discovery, that he be examined also as the representative of
the Congress and that he pay special costs of his “re-attendance”.

[
4
]

The defendant, relying upon Rule 18A, seeks to
have the action against Dr. Elterman dismissed and pursuant to Rule 19(11)
seeks further and better particulars of the allegations of publication.

[
5
]

I will begin by dealing with the defendant’s
applications.

THE CLAIM FOR PARTICULARS

[
6
]

The defendant seeks further and better
particulars of paragraphs 5 and 6 of the Statement of Claim in order to
formulate its defence.  Though the motion referred only to those two paragraphs
it seems apparent from the argument that the defendant also seeks particulars
of paragraph 7.  These paragraphs read as follows:

5.   The defendants, and each of them, in the
first half of the year ... 1998 caused a brochure to issue over its name, and
with its imprimatur entitled “CANADIAN JEWISH CONGRESS PACIFIC REGION - Issues
of Concern to the Jewish Community of British Columbia 1995-1998”.

6.   As a sub topic in the publication referred
to above, a chapter was published under the title HATE GROUPS AND HATE PROPAGANDA.
This chapter contained the following paragraph regarding the plaintiff:  “While
strongly tied to American hate groups, the White Supremacist movement in Canada
has an identity distinct from its southern neighbors.  Homosexuals, Jews, South
Asians, African Canadians and other groups have been the targets of violence
and hate propaganda by groups like the Western Guard, the Northern Hammerskins,
the Heritage Front, Canadian League of Rights, Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
(C-Far), the National Party of Canada (NPOC), the Church of the Creator, and
the Council on Public Affairs, etc.  Canadian hate groups often promote
themselves as legitimate and academic movements, usually under the guise of
free speech, grassroots advocacy on public policy issues or Holocaust
revisionism.”

7.   The foregoing publication was widely
distributed to Judges, lawyers, police officials, and important
decision-makers, as well as the public, in a distribution known to the
defendant, but details of which are presently unknown to the plaintiff.  This
publication was done in British Columbia where the “Pacific Region" has
its headquarters, and primarily circulated the brochure in British Columbia.
The foregoing paragraph was extremely defamatory ...

[
7
]

The defendant claims that particulars regarding
the details of publication and distribution are necessary in order to properly
formulate its defence.  A general defence denying all allegations has been
filed, but the defence intends to amend to plead justification, fair comment,
qualified privilege, and/or absolute privilege.  The defendant is also
considering asserting the truth of the impugned statements, another potential
defence, showing that the plaintiff is in fact an extremist organization, that
does engage in acts of hate and violence towards minority groups.  Finally, it
intends to plead that the plaintiff has not suffered any loss of reputation and
is incapable of suffering such a loss.

[
8
]

Before discoveries took place, the defendant
made a request for particulars regarding the alleged publication, but the
plaintiff declined to provide any.  Counsel for the defendant argues that
merely claiming the document was sent to “judges, lawyers and decision makers”
is not sufficient.  It must characterize how it was directed to them and, depending
upon the delivery (if any), a particular defence might be alleged.  As an
example, counsel said that if the document was produced to a judge during a
legal submission it might attract privilege.  If it was given to a lawyer for a
purpose then depending upon that purpose, a defence might arise.

[
9
]

It is argued for the defence that it is
incumbent upon the plaintiff to particularize the method of publication.  In
this regard counsel relies upon
Wesson v. Campbell River and District
(Pacific 317) Branch of the Royal Canadian Legion
,
Taggart and
Weis
,
1985 CanLII 479 (BC CA)
, 63 B.C.L.R. 327 (B.C.C.A.).

[
10
]

In
Wesson
, the claim of publication was not specified
beyond “divers persons” and the defendant was successful in obtaining an order
from a Chambers Judge for further and better particulars.  However, the order
stated that such particulars were to be provided “following completion of the
plaintiff’s discovery examination of the defendants” and it was from that order
that the defendants appealed.  The Court of Appeal reversed this aspect of the
order.

[
11
]

In
Wesson
,
Taggart J.A. (at 330) quotes from
Gatley on Libel and Slander, 8th ed. (1981) at para. 1067.  That paragraph
reads as follows:

1067.  Publication to persons unknown.  If the
plaintiff knows or believes that the words have been published on more
occasions and to more persons than he is at present aware of, he should state
the names of the persons to whom he knows the words were published, and
continue:  “The plaintiff believes that the said words were also published to
some other persons whom he cannot at present specify, but he will rely upon the
publication thereof to every person to whom he may discover the same to have
been published.”  But unless the plaintiff can show clearly that there have
been other publications, the court will order particulars of the names and
addresses of such other persons, or in default that the allegation be struck
out; nor will the court postpone the giving of such particulars until after
discovery and interrogatories.  The plaintiff may not interrogate the defendant
in order to discover instances of publication of which he is unable to give
particulars, unless he can show by uncontradicted affidavit that there has been
such publication.

[
12
]

This passage

was also quoted by Shabbits J. in
Walker
v.

C.R.O.S.

(1993), 18 C.C.L.T. (2d) 166 at 172 (B.C.S.C.)
.  In that
case, the statement of claim alleged that the defendants had sent a defamatory
“information package” to “members of
C.R.O.S.
[an unorganized group of
Surrey residents] and other unknown persons in South Surrey”.  Shabbits J.
determined that the defendant was entitled to particulars as to who was given
copies of the information package before the discovery process took place.

[
13
]

The plaintiff referred to a number of cases on this issue, only two
of which involve claims for defamation.   One of these two addresses the issue
of publication and also refers to
Wesson
, supra
.  Allan J.
in
Richardson
v.
Norton

Lilly International (Canada) Ltd.

[1993] B.C.J. No. 1890 (Q.L.)
determined that as there was evidence the
defendant had made defamatory remarks to persons within the industry in
question, and that the defendant was the only one who knew to whom those
remarks were made, it was impossible for the plaintiff to provide any “better
particulars”.

[
14
]

In my view the situation in
Richardson
, supra
,
is far removed from the one at bar.  Unlike the
Richardson
case,
there is no evidence whatever before me to establish that the impugned document
was ever “published”.   Counsel for the plaintiff suggests that given the
stated objectives of the document, I can assume publication, much as one can
assume a newspaper is widely distributed because of its claims of circulation.
I am unable to accept that proposition.

[
15
]

I have concluded that in this case, the defendant’s demand for
particulars is justified. The defendant has, in my view, shown that the
particulars sought are necessary to enable them to properly prepare their case,
and so fit within those listed in Rule 19(11).  Here there is a bald assertion
that the document was widely distributed to “judges, lawyers, police officials,
and important decision-makers, as well as the public ...”   There is nothing to
suggest that the defendant has any “peculiar knowledge” about distribution.
If, as claimed, it was “widely distributed”, then surely the plaintiff can
provide those particulars.

[
16
]

In exercising my discretion, I have considered whether the
particulars should be given before or after the discovery process.  Regarding
this issue, Taggart J.A. in
Wesson
, supra
at p. 331, stated:

Before the plaintiff completes his examination
for discovery of the defendants I think they are entitled to know what is the
plaintiff’s case on the issue of publication.  And I think, furthermore, they
are entitled to know that in the terms of the order appealed from, that is to
say, “including further and better particulars of when and in what
circumstances and by whom and to whom the allegedly defamatory words were
published”.  I think the chambers judge erred in deferring the particulars
until after the discovery of the defendants by the plaintiff has been
completed.  Accordingly, I would allow the appeal and direct that the
particulars be provided before the examination for discovery has been
completed.  I would, however, give the plaintiff 30 days within which to
provide the particulars requested....

[
17
]

Esson J.A. agreed and added comments relative to a defamation
action.  On p. 331 he stated:

I agree, but would add only this: in general
there is a wide discretion to order that the giving of particulars be postponed
until after discovery.  The scope of that discretion is much narrower in a
defamation action than in most, if not all other classes of action.  Normally
an application of this kind should be brought before discovery and not, as
here, after the plaintiff and two or three defendants have been examined.  In
some circumstances that would be sufficient to justify postponing the
particulars until completion of the discovery, but this action falls so clearly
into the category of a fishing expedition that the defendants should not have
to submit to any further discovery unless and until the particulars are given.
If particulars cannot be given, the likely result will be to bring the action
to an end at this stage.  If the plaintiff can put forward no more concrete
case than he has to this point that is an appropriate outcome.

[
18
]

A party must frame its pleadings with certainty and must, to the
extent possible, set out the facts, but not the evidence, on which they intend
to rely.  In the present case, the statement of claim does not allow the
defendant to know to whom the publication was sent, or the manner in which it
was distributed, assuming distribution.

[
19
]

I therefore conclude that the plaintiff must provide particulars of
publication and distribution before discoveries continue in order to permit the
plaintiff to respond appropriately.  Without such particulars, the plaintiff’s
assertion that the publication was widely distributed to "judges, lawyers,
police officials, and important decision-makers, as well as the public..."
is no more than mere speculation.  Specifically, with respect to paragraph 7 of
the statement of claim, the plaintiff must supply particulars known to the
plaintiff of the names of the people to whom the publication was allegedly
distributed and any other known details about how the publication was directed
to these individuals.

THE 18A APPLICATION

[
20
]

Dr. Elterman has deposed that he is a volunteer with the Canadian
Jewish Congress, Pacific Region in Vancouver.  He described the Pacific Region
as a “branch office” of the national organization.

[
21
]

Although Dr. Elterman admitted the document was prepared during his
tenure as Chair, he denied any involvement in its drafting, publication or
distribution, claiming that the final decision to release it was made “by the
committee which I chaired but as chairman I did not provide any input as to the
contents of the document or as to the use of that document.”

[
22
]

He then specifically denied that the document was issued over his
name and denied that he had any involvement in drafting the impugned
paragraph.  He did, however, concede that though he did not actually sign the
“Forward”, his name, as Chair, was placed thereon with his approval.

[
23
]

The “Forward” contains five paragraphs that essentially set forth
the objectives of the defendant Congress.  Two of these paragraphs, which are
relevant to the present circumstances, read as follows:

Canadian Jewish Congress, Pacific Region works
with and maintains close links with all provincial parties and all levels of
government.  We have prepared
this document
[emphasis added] in an
effort to familiarize and sensitize all political parties and levels of
government to the issues of concern to British Columbia’s Jewish community.
In addition, we have prepared a number of recommended actions relating to each
issue.

We believe that the members of British
Columbia’s Jewish community have an important role to play in the political
process, both as citizens of the province and as members of a cultural, ethnic
and religious community.  We believe that this initiative will contribute to
the creation of a more open and just society.

[
24
]

I am unable to accept counsel’s contention that Dr. Elterman’s
affidavit stating that he neither drafted, published nor distributed the
document is, in the absence of some contrary material submitted by the
plaintiff, sufficient evidence upon which to resolve the 18A issue in the
defendant’s favour.  Dr. Elterman concedes that the Forward, which clearly
refers to the impugned document, did “go out under my name”.  He specifically
adopts the actions of a Mr. Nest, who apparently appended Dr. Elterman’s
signature to the Forward.  In a somewhat circuitous fashion, Dr. Elterman
concedes the Forward is his responsibility.

[
25
]

No submission was advanced before me that Dr. Elterman was not a
proper party.  Rather, the thrust of the motion was that since he deposed that
he had nothing to do with the preparation or production of the impugned
document, the action against him ought to be dismissed.  However, the Forward
is admittedly in his name and it adopts the impugned document.  Thus if
publication and distribution can be established, and the document is found to
be defamatory, Dr. Elterman might be liable along with the Congress.

[
26
]

It might well transpire that though Dr. Elterman did not prepare, or
personally arrange for distribution, by his adoption of the material and his
knowledge of the distribution, he attracts liability.  Those are matters to be
resolved once particulars are furnished and the pleadings are amended.

EXAMINATION FOR DISCOVERY OF DR.
ELTERMAN

[
27
]

The plaintiff seeks an order compelling Dr. Elterman to answer a
series of questions posed to him in his examination for discovery.

[
28
]

In my view, notwithstanding Dr. Elterman’s denial contained in his
affidavit of any involvement in the drafting, publication or distribution of
the impugned material, the plaintiff ought to be entitled to examine him to
test those denials.

[
29
]

Initially, the defendant objected to the plaintiff’s demand to
discover Dr. Elterman as the representative of the defendant Congress.  Now,
however it appears that counsel has conceded that Dr. Elterman is a proper
person to be examined in that capacity.   In the result, some questions put to
Dr. Elterman at his discovery as a personal defendant, would not now be
objectionable in his representational capacity.

[
30
]

The defendant also initially objected to the plaintiff’s demand to
discover Dr. Elterman due to the plaintiff’s failure to provide further
particulars regarding the publication and distribution of the impugned
material.  With regard to these issues, I do not propose to define the
permissible questions.  Rather, I will leave it to counsel to come to an
agreement after considering the import of my decision on other issues.  If no
agreement can be reached, then counsel have liberty to apply.

CONCLUSION

[
31
]

The defendant is entitled to the particulars requested. The
application to dismiss the claim against Dr. Elterman is denied.  The precise
questions appropriate to a continued discovery should be resolved by counsel
but failing resolution, the parties have leave to apply.

[
32
]

If the parties wish to speak to the issue of costs they have liberty
to do so.  They will otherwise be in the cause.

"R.A. McKinnon, J."

The Honourable Mr. Justice R.A. McKinnon
